text:
You've probably seen the video. A young Frenchwoman in Paris, in tears, begging looters to stop. "Why are you doing this? That's not what we stand for."

Some accounts are mocking her. "She voted for it."

I won't. Because what you see on her face is not stupidity. It's a disease that has infected the entire West, and it has a name: suicidal empathy.

The term comes from Gad Saad, an evolutionary behavioral scientist at Concordia University in Montreal. A man who fled the Lebanese civil war as a child, and who knows what it looks like when a society falls apart. His new book, Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind, is the follow-up to The Parasitic Mind. Here is the thesis, and why it concerns every one of us.

Empathy is one of the best things about us. It evolved for a reason: to care for our children, our kin, our tribe. It was calibrated for a world where the people you felt for were the people around you, and where empathy always came paired with its counterweight: the instinct to protect your own and to recognize a threat.

Suicidal empathy is what happens when that mechanism misfires. When it fires at the wrong targets, in the wrong amounts, with no brake. When we feel more for the criminal than for his victim. More for the stranger who breaks the rules than for the citizen who follows them. More for how compassionate we look than for what our compassion actually produces.

Where does it come from? Four layers.

First, biology. Empathy is a spotlight, as the psychologist Paul Bloom put it. It lights up the one face in front of you and leaves everything else in the dark. The crying migrant on the boat is visible. The thousands of future victims of a broken system are statistics. A spotlight is a terrible tool for running a country.

Second, our own civilization. The West is the civilization that put the victim at the center of its morality. Christianity taught us to care for the stranger, the poor, the weak. It was one of the greatest moral revolutions in history. But cut off from its other half, justice, responsibility, the duty to protect your own, it turns into something else.

Third, ideology. In The Parasitic Mind, Saad described idea pathogens, ideas that hijack our reasoning. Suicidal empathy is the emotional counterpart: an ideology that hijacks our compassion. It sorts the world into oppressors and victims, then demands unlimited empathy for whoever ranks as the victim, whatever they do.

Fourth, status. In the age of social media, empathy has become a display. Posting "refugees welcome" costs nothing and earns applause. The bill goes to someone else: the working class, the suburbs, the women walking home at night.

The results are everywhere. Criminals treated as victims of society. Sexual assaults by migrants met with lenient sentences. Self-defense branded as aggression. Borders treated as cruelty. Saad's conclusion is simple: a society dies when it would rather display infinite tolerance than use its survival instinct.

Now the part I'll add myself, and that few people dare to say.

On average, women score higher than men on measures of empathy. It's one of the most consistent findings in psychology, across cultures, and it makes perfect evolutionary sense: for most of human history, the survival of children depended on it. It's a strength.

But it means an ideology that weaponizes empathy will hit women harder. And the data shows it: in country after country, young women have moved sharply to the left of young men, especially on immigration.

This is where men have a responsibility.

Not to mock. Not to lecture. Not to say "she deserved it." Empathy has always needed a counterweight, and that counterweight was the protective instinct: the one that draws lines, says no, and stands between the threat and the people it loves.

Men abandoned that role. They were told it was toxic, and many believed it. So they stayed silent at the dinner table, at work, with their partners, sisters, daughters and friends.

That has to end. Men have to have this conversation, honestly and with respect: compassion that cannot say no is not compassion. It's surrender. And the first to pay for it are women.

Many women already understand this better than anyone. Some of the bravest voices in this fight are women, precisely because they are the first to feel the danger in the street.

A civilization rests on a balance: compassion and strength, openness and borders, mercy and justice. When one side swallows the other, the foundations crack. What we are watching in Europe is what happens when empathy has no counterweight left.

Look at that young woman again. She isn't the enemy. She's what this ideology made of a generation that was told kindness would be enough.

Our job is to make sure she's the last generation that has to learn it this way.

quoted_tweet.author: Erik Dale 🇳🇴
quoted_tweet.text:
She voted for it.
She welcomed them.

Faced with the encore, she begs them to stop. In her heart she knows they will not.

Everything she believed. That they were French like her, fighting for the same cause. That the ones who warned her were full of hate. That she would be safe.

It all falls apart in this moment. She is terrified of what comes next. In her heart she knows.

Only remigration can save her.

Starlink became a lifeline when a sailor suffered a stroke with no mobile signal. ♥️

Elliot Russo was aboard his yacht in a remote Indonesian lagoon, when he lost movement on one side and struggled to speak.

There was no mobile coverage. Their Starlink connection let them contact an emergency medical team, share their location and reach people who helped arrange a rescue. A boat arrived with medics and took Elliot to hospital. He survived and later recovered.

This is why Starlink matters. It helps save lives. This life-saving technology should be available in every part of the world.

AI狂热、市场定价与长期回报

李录：

市场从一开始就一直会做一些很奇怪的事情。过去如此，将来也大概会继续如此。

但市场在任何一个时点决定做什么，其实完全没有必要支配你的行为。这恰恰是本·格雷厄姆最重要的洞见之一，也是他对投资世界最重要的贡献之一。

比如说，我最近看过一份募资材料。有一家公司把自己称作“研究实验室”。它现在每年烧掉数百亿美元，同时还承诺，未来会继续烧掉数千亿美元。

它告诉你，它正在创造一种具有变革性的技术；但与此同时，它又说，这项技术有大约10%的概率把所有人都杀死。

这些话就写在募资材料里。

然后，它邀请所有人至少投入1000亿美元，并且按照2万亿美元的估值来给它定价。如果这里面存在任何逻辑上的一致性，那已经很令人费解了。

这其实是一个非常极端的例子，说明市场有时候能够非理性到什么程度。这些事情不可能同时都是真的，但市场现在就是到了这种位置。

这也说明，这种状态不可能以一种理性的方式长期持续下去。如果你回头看几百年的市场历史，就会发现，市场的确会在相当长的一段时间里做非常奇怪的事情。

举个例子。从2010年开始算，过去大约16年里，标普500的年化回报大约有14%到15%。但是在此前的10年，也就是2000年到2010年，它的年化回报几乎正好是0，甚至略微为负。如果把这26年放在一起看，长期年化回报大致又回到了高个位数。

这其实差不多就是合理的长期水平。

你想一想：在这段时间里，实际GDP增长可能大约2%；再加上2%到3%左右的通胀，合在一起，名义经济增速大约就是4%到5%。

而上市公司通常会比整体经济表现稍好一些，尤其像标普500这样，它本身经过筛选，留下的是大约500家最优秀的企业。所以最后得到一个高个位数的长期回报，并不奇怪。

而这恰恰就是市场长期以来的平均水平。所以，这应该成为一个非常重要的基础锚点：你长期究竟应该得到什么样的回报，以及市场最终会怎样回归理性。

但是在这个长期趋势之间，市场会不断出现一段一段的偏离。有时候，这种偏离还会持续非常长的时间，并且走向极端。

我们刚才举的那个例子，至少会让人觉得非常反常。但这种事情确实会发生，而且历史上一直都在发生。
